intro: To reset Chrome settings on a Mac, click the More icon (three dots), choose Settings, then click Reset settings and Restore settings to their original defaults. Click Reset settings again to confirm, and expect your bookmarks and saved passwords to stay put.
tldr: Open Settings from the More icon (three dots) in the top-right corner, or press ⌘ ,.
Choose Reset settings, then Restore settings to their original defaults, then Reset settings again to confirm.
Bookmarks and saved passwords stay. Cookies, your homepage, your search engine and extensions go back to defaults.
The reset applies to every device where you are signed in, so check your other computers too.

blocks.text: Reset Chrome settings on a Mac, step by step

Chrome keeps its main controls on one Settings page. The reset lives on that same page, so you do not need Terminal or a third-party tool. Google's help page describes the steps for desktop Chrome, and the steps below follow it. Labels can shift a little between releases, so match the wording you see on your screen.

Start by opening Chrome and making sure it is the window you want to reset. Then click the More icon in the top-right corner. It looks like three dots. A menu drops down, and Settings is in that menu. If you prefer the keyboard, press ⌘ , and Settings opens in a new tab.
What the reset changes in Chrome

The reset sends a specific list of things back to their defaults. Google names these on its help page. The table below gives you the list in plain terms, so you can decide what you will need to set up again.

rows: New tab page and pinned tabs
Content settings, such as pop-up and microphone permissions
blocks.caption: What Google's Chrome Help page says the reset does

blocks.text: Pay attention to extensions and themes. They are part of the reset, so the add-ons you use every day may look different afterward. Write down the ones you rely on before you start, so you can add them back.

The reset also follows you to other devices. Google says it applies across every device where you are signed in. If you reset on your Mac, your other signed-in computers and phones can change too. Plan for that, especially if you share a Google account with someone else.
A worked example of a reset

Take a common case. Your homepage keeps changing, your searches go to a search engine you never picked, and an exception that lets your bank's site open pop-ups has stopped working. A reset targets exactly that kind of drift, because the homepage, the search engine and content settings all sit on the list above.

After the reset, the homepage and search engine are back to Chrome's defaults. You then add back the bank exception in that site's own permission settings. Your bookmarks and saved passwords were never touched, so your bank login is still there once you sign in again.
What the reset keeps, and what Google does not say

Bookmarks and saved passwords are not deleted or changed by the reset, according to Google. Fonts and accessibility options are kept as well. Those points matter most if you were worried about losing your logins or your saved sites.

Google's page does not mention browsing history. Some third-party guides disagree about passwords and history, so do not rely on them for those two items. Treat your history as uncertain, and check it after the reset. A reset is also not a full reset, as the section on fresh starts explains.
Check these four things before you click Reset

items: Make sure you know the password for your Google account, in case Chrome asks you to sign in again.
Confirm that sync is on, and that you are signed in to the account you expect.
List the extensions you use every day, because extensions and themes go back to defaults too.
Note your homepage, default search engine and any site permissions you rely on, such as the microphone or pop-ups.

blocks.text: Each check takes a few minutes. It saves you from guessing later which setting you changed, and it gives you a list to rebuild from.
Why Chrome settings get changed in the first place

Chrome is the most used desktop browser, so its settings draw a lot of attention. StatCounter measured Chrome at 66.98% of worldwide desktop browser market share in October 2026. In the United States, Chrome held 62.63% of desktop browser share that month.

Not every change comes from you. Socket reported on October 29, 2026 that it found 319 Chrome extensions, many of them search hijackers. Those extensions were installed by roughly 13.4 million users over a decade.

That 13.4 million figure is a total across a decade, not a count of people who still have the extensions today. Still, it shows why a reset can be the right move. If a setting keeps coming back, the cause may sit in your extension list, not in Chrome itself.
Keyboard shortcuts for Settings and history

The Mac shortcut ⌘ , opens Settings in a new tab. It is the fastest way in, and it skips the More menu. Google's shortcut page also lists ⌘ Y for History and ⌘ ⇧ J for Downloads, each in a new tab. Google does not list a shortcut for the reset itself, so you still click through the Reset settings section.
Fix the reset when it does not work

Most reset problems come from one of three places. The Settings menu may be broken, a program on your Mac may be changing settings, or an organization may control the browser. Google's help page covers the first two. The third needs more care, and it gets its own section below.

If the Settings menu is missing or will not open, Google suggests removing Chrome and reinstalling it from google.com/chrome. That is the official fix. Once Chrome opens again, go back to Settings and run the reset as normal.

If the reset works but a setting comes back, look for a program you installed. Google says a program you installed may be changing Chrome settings. Review your extensions, remove anything you do not recognize, and then check the setting once more.
Reset Chrome settings on a work Mac or managed browser

If Chrome shows Managed by your organization, a policy is controlling some settings. A guide from Guiding Tech, updated August 8, 2024, says to check chrome://policy to see which policies are active. The same guide says a reset plus disabling extensions can help.

Be careful on a company Mac. Do not remove policies without your IT team. A policy that looks wrong may be there for a reason, such as security or a required setting. Ask first, and keep a note of what you changed.
If you want a true fresh start

A reset is not a full reset. Google says that to start fresh, you should add a new user profile in Chrome. A new profile starts with its own bookmarks, passwords and settings. Your old profile stays as it is. Learn how in [how to create a Chrome profile](/how-to/create-a-chrome-profile-in-chrome).
Mistakes people make with a Chrome reset

items: Resetting to fix one site. A single site permission is usually faster to change in that site's own settings.
Expecting history to disappear. Google does not list history, so check it yourself.
Resetting while an extension is the real cause. The setting returns, and you have lost time and your list of add-ons.
Forgetting the other devices. Your other signed-in computers can change together with your Mac.
Skipping the sign-in check. Cookies and site data are reset, so some sites ask you to sign in again.

blocks.text: What to do right after the reset

Open a new tab and look at the page that appears. Set your homepage and default search engine again if you want them. Then check your permissions for the microphone and pop-ups, because those are part of the reset.

Next, reinstall only the extensions you actually use. Add them one at a time and check your settings after each one. If a setting changes after one install, you have found the cause. For a stricter setup, see [how to block third-party cookies in Chrome](/how-to/block-third-party-cookies-in-chrome). To add an extension back, read [how to install an extension in Chrome](/how-to/install-an-extension-in-chrome).

faq.question: Does resetting Chrome settings on Mac delete my bookmarks?
faq.answer: No. Google's help page says saved bookmarks and saved passwords are not deleted or changed by the reset. Fonts and accessibility options are kept as well. If bookmarks look missing, check which Google account you are signed in to.

faq.question: Does the reset clear my browsing history?
faq.answer: Google's reset page does not list browsing history, so do not count on either result. Some third-party guides disagree about history and passwords. Check your history after the reset, and treat any clean-up as a separate step.

faq.question: Will the reset change Chrome on my other computers?
faq.answer: It can. Google says the reset applies across every device where you are signed in. If you reset on your Mac, your other signed-in computers and phones may change too.

faq.question: Is there a keyboard shortcut to reset Chrome settings?
faq.answer: Google's keyboard shortcut page lists ⌘ , for opening Settings in a new tab. It does not list a shortcut for the reset itself. Press ⌘ , to get to Settings quickly, then follow the Reset settings section.

faq.question: What is the difference between a reset and a new profile?
faq.answer: A reset returns settings to defaults, but it is not a full reset. A new user profile gives you a clean start with its own bookmarks, passwords and settings. Google's page says to add a new profile for a fresh start.

faq.question: Why is the Settings menu missing in Chrome on my Mac?
faq.answer: Google's help page says Chrome may have a problem if the Settings menu is missing or does not open. The official fix is to remove Chrome and reinstall it from google.com/chrome.

faq.question: Why does a Chrome setting stay locked after a reset?
faq.answer: Your Mac may be managed by an organization. Check chrome://policy to see which policies apply. On a company Mac, speak to your IT team before you change or remove any policy.

requirements: A Mac with Google Chrome installed and open
A signed-in Google account, if you use sync
About five minutes and a quick check of your extensions

steps.name: Open Chrome and check the window
steps.text: Open Google Chrome on your Mac. The reset covers the browser as a whole, so any window works. Make sure you are signed in with the account you use every day, because the reset also reaches your other signed-in devices.
steps.tip: Write down your homepage and search engine before you start.

steps.name: Open the More menu
steps.text: Click the More icon in the top-right corner of the Chrome window. It looks like three dots. A menu opens below it.
steps.tip: The icon sits to the right of the address bar.

steps.name: Choose Settings
steps.text: Click Settings in the menu. Chrome opens its Settings page. You can also press ⌘ , to skip the menu.
steps.tip: The shortcut opens Settings in a new tab.

steps.name: Open Reset settings
steps.text: On the Settings page, click Reset settings. Google uses this exact label, so look for it by name.
steps.tip: If the page does not open, read the troubleshooting section below.

steps.name: Pick the restore option
steps.text: Click Restore settings to their original defaults. This is the option that sends the settings listed above back to defaults. Read the wording before you go on.
steps.tip: Bookmarks and saved passwords are not deleted, according to Google.

steps.name: Confirm the reset
steps.text: Click Reset settings in the confirmation dialog. The reset applies to this Mac and to each device where you are signed in.
steps.tip: Check your requirements list before this step, because the settings go back to defaults at this point.

steps.name: Check the result
steps.text: Look at your homepage, your search engine and your new tab page. Then open a site where you use a permission, such as a video call site, and check that it asks you again.
steps.tip: Re-add extensions one at a time so you can spot a setting that changes back.

troubleshooting.problem: Settings menu is missing or will not open
troubleshooting.fix: Google suggests removing Chrome and reinstalling it from google.com/chrome. Then open Settings again and run the reset.

troubleshooting.problem: The setting comes back after the reset
troubleshooting.fix: A program you installed may be changing Chrome's settings. Review extensions and recent installs, remove anything you do not recognize, then check the setting again.
Check chrome://policy to see which policies apply. On a work Mac, ask your IT team before you remove any policy.
Google says the reset does not delete bookmarks or saved passwords. Check that you are signed in to the right Google account and that sync is on.

troubleshooting.problem: Sites ask you to sign in again
troubleshooting.fix: Cookies and site data are part of the reset, so this is expected. Sign in once per site, and the cookies come back as you use each site.

troubleshooting.problem: You want history or a clean slate
troubleshooting.fix: Google's page does not list history for the reset. For a clean start, add a new user profile in Chrome instead.
